hints: To land on rung i you must have come from rung i−1 or rung i−2. If you already knew the cheapest cost to stand on those two, could you work out rung i?
1D DP: cost[i] = toll[i] + min(cost[i−1], cost[i−2]). The top is reached from either of the last two rungs. Only the last two values are needed, so two variables are enough.

1. a = toll[0], b = toll[1] (cheapest cost to stand on rungs 0 and 1).
  2. For i = 2..n−1: c = toll[i] + min(a, b); shift a = b, b = c.
  3. Return min(a, b) — step to the top from either of the last two rungs.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Recursively try a 1-step and a 2-step from every rung.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Same recursion with memoization (or a dp array).

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Bottom-up DP keeping only the last two values.

explain: For toll [4,9,2]: standing on rung 0 costs 4, rung 1 costs 9, rung 2 costs 2 + min(4, 9) = 6. The top is reached from rung 1 or 2, so the answer is min(9, 6) = 6. Each rung's cost only depends on the two below it, which is why we can throw older values away. If the ladder has a single rung, the answer is just min of what we have — guard for length 1.
recognize: Minimum cost to reach the end when each step goes 1 or 2 places forward → 1D DP over the last two states.
